title: Eighth commandment (CCC 2464–2499)
hook: truth, reputation and not spreading faults

segments.voice: Yesterday, stewardship: the earth and its creatures, held in trust. Your line was entrusted. What did you look after, that wasn't yours? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

"Did you hear about Dan?" Five words, and the room leans in. What comes next might even be true. Dan did lose his temper at the meeting. Dan's marriage is in trouble. Nobody is lying. And yet, by the end of lunch, a whole table of people who will never help Dan think a little less of him, and Dan doesn't know it happened. The Catechism has a name for that, and it isn't lying. It sits under the commandment about truth. Today: the eighth commandment, and why it guards more than facts.
screen: `DID YOU HEAR ABOUT DAN?` → `NOBODY IS LYING.` → `DAN DOESN'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: The commandment itself, from Exodus in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." A courtroom picture. Someone stands up and lies, and an innocent person pays. The Catechism calls truthfulness the virtue of being true in what we do and say, and of guarding against two-facedness. But then it widens the frame, and this is where it gets uncomfortable. It names three sins against a person's reputation. First, rash judgment: assuming the worst about someone without enough to go on. Second, calumny: saying false things that damage them. Third, detraction. Detraction is telling someone else's real faults to people who didn't know them, without a serious reason. Real faults. True things. Dan really did lose his temper. The Catechism still counts it as a wrong, because a good name belongs to a person, and you can take it from them with the truth. It even offers a habit for the other side. Quoting Saint Ignatius of Loyola, it says a Christian should be readier to give a good reading to what a neighbor says than to condemn it, and if the words seem wrong, to ask what was meant. And when harm is done, the Catechism says it has to be repaired, even if the one who caused it has been forgiven. That can be hard: walking back into the lunchroom and saying, I shouldn't have said that about Dan. Notice one more thing. The Catechism also says not everyone has a right to every truth. Some things are kept for love's sake, or for safety, or under a seal, like the confessional. Truth, in this commandment, is not a weapon for whoever wants one.
screen: `NO FALSE WITNESS.` · `RASH JUDGMENT, CALUMNY, DETRACTION.` · `TRUE FAULTS CAN STILL WOUND.` · `THE HARM MUST BE REPAIRED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't repeat one piece of gossip. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you know about someone, true or half true, that you've been tempted to pass on. Don't replay the details. Just hold the person's name. Picture them walking into the room right now. Then picture the story staying with you, set down, not passed along. If you pray, you can ask God to guard their good name. If you don't, just let the story end with you. The bell holds the time.

The eighth commandment. You shall not bear false witness: in Catholic teaching, a call to live in the truth, and to guard every neighbor's good name, even from true things told without need. Today's word.
Your line: guard reputations. Today, when a conversation turns to someone who isn't there, say one good true thing about them, or change the subject. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics examine themselves on the eighth commandment before confession, asking about lies, rash judgment, calumny and detraction; the Church teaches that harm done to a reputation should be repaired where possible.

fork.setup: at lunch, a coworker says, "did you hear about Dan?" what you know is true, and nobody else at the table knows it. what does the Catechism call passing it on without a serious reason?
fork.reveal: detraction: revealing another's real faults to people who didn't know them. calumny is when the thing said is false.

trapdoor: what you thought: the eighth commandment means don't lie.
what it means: live in the truth, and guard every neighbor's good name, even from true things told without need.
what a scholar hears: a courtroom law about false testimony, which the Catechism widens to rash judgment, calumny and detraction, with a duty to repair.
recall: a firm habit of doing good
